candidates.quote: To have some account of my thoughts, manners, acquaintance and actions, when the hour arrives in which time is more nimble than memory, is the reason which induces me to keep a Journal. A Journal in which I must confess my every thought, must open my whole heart!
candidates.author: Frances Burney
candidates.work: The Early Diary of Frances Burney
candidates.locator: the first entry, Poland Street, London, 27 March 1768 (ed. Annie Raine Ellis, 1889), vol. I, p. 4
candidates.whyThisMonth: A girl of fifteen sets the terms of honest writing before she has written anything: the page gets every thought or it gets nothing.

candidates.quote: If this book be not the exact, the absolute, the strict truth, it has no right to exist.
candidates.author: Marie Bashkirtseff
candidates.whyThisMonth: She stakes the whole worth of a life's writing on one condition, and the reader can apply the same test to a morning.

candidates.quote: The question is not what you look at, but what you see.
candidates.author: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.locator: entry of 5 August 1851 (ed. Bradford Torrey and Francis H. Allen, 1906)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Eleven words that move the whole burden of a day from the world onto the attention that meets it.

candidates.quote: All letters, methinks, should be free and easy as one’s discourse; not studied as an oration, nor made up of hard words like a charm.
candidates.author: Dorothy Osborne
candidates.work: Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple
candidates.whyThisMonth: The best plain-speech rule in English was written by a woman telling her lover to stop performing, and it still works on anything about to be sent.

candidates.quote: How odd it is that every one should not see that all observation must be for or against some view, if it is to be of any service.
candidates.author: Charles Darwin
candidates.whyThisMonth: Clear seeing is not blank seeing: Darwin says plainly that looking at anything usefully means having something at stake in it.

candidates.quote: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligation where no benefit has been received, or to be unwilling that the Public should consider me as owing that to a Patron, which Providence has enabled me to do for myself.
candidates.author: Samuel Johnson
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most courteous refusal in English to pretend a gratitude one does not feel: the exact opposite of a wound, and the exact shape of a true sentence.

candidates.quote: I do not enjoy making ‘desolation,’ believe me, but I cannot change my eyes!
candidates.author: Gustave Flaubert
candidates.locator: letter CCCI, December 1875, in The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters
candidates.whyThisMonth: Answering a friend who wanted him to console rather than describe, he admits the one thing nobody can trade away, which is how he sees.

candidates.quote: I’ll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination.
candidates.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
candidates.locator: chapter 1, the opening sentence of the novel
candidates.whyThisMonth: It opens the month by refusing the easy split between an accurate report and a true one, which is the honest starting point for anyone about to describe a day.
candidates.speaker: Genly Ai

candidates.quote: To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.
candidates.author: Jorge Luis Borges
candidates.locator: the closing section of the story, in Labyrinths (New Directions, 1962)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man who could forget nothing could think about nothing: a quiet warning that clarity is built by leaving things out.
candidates.speaker: the narrator

candidates.quote: ‘But he hasn’t got anything on,’ a little child said.
candidates.author: Hans Christian Andersen
candidates.locator: the procession, near the close of the tale
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest picture we have of plain speech: one small voice describing what is in front of everybody, and no cruelty in it at all.
candidates.speaker: a little child

candidates.quote: He could see plainly that she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself and daily casting aside that fictitious self which we assume like a garment with which to appear before the world.
candidates.author: Kate Chopin
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence turns on the difference between looking at someone and seeing them, and it names the garment most of us are already putting on at six.

candidates.quote: Hundreds of people can talk for one who can think, but thousands can think for one who can see. To see clearly is poetry, prophecy, and religion,—all in one.
candidates.author: John Ruskin
candidates.locator: Part IV, chapter XVI, Of Modern Landscape, section 28
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month's own thesis, stated by the man who spent his life on it: seeing is rarer than thinking and worth more.

candidates.quote: Good prose is like a window pane.
candidates.author: George Orwell
candidates.locator: the closing page, in Gangrel, No. 4, Summer 1946
candidates.whyThisMonth: Six words that set the standard for every sentence the reader will say or write today: you should be able to see through it.

candidates.quote: I wished to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it.
candidates.author: Anne Brontë
candidates.locator: Preface to the Second Edition, 22 July 1848
candidates.whyThisMonth: A writer answering critics who wanted her to soften things says the plainest version of this month's case, that truth needs no decoration to do its work.

candidates.quote: The writer should never be ashamed of staring. There is nothing that doesn’t require his attention.
candidates.author: Flannery O’Connor
candidates.locator: The Nature and Aim of Fiction, p. 84
candidates.whyThisMonth: Permission to look at things longer than is polite, which is exactly the practice a morning of clear seeing asks for.

candidates.quote: I shall be employed about things, not words!
candidates.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
candidates.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
candidates.whyThisMonth: She announces in the first pages that she will not polish her style, and the vow itself is the cleanest sentence in the book.
